\chapter{Theoretical Background}
\label{ch:background}

This chapter assembles the minimum theory the thesis rests on, in the
order the methodology uses it: neutron multiplication and its leakage
hierarchy, fuel depletion and the role of the burnable absorber, the
power-peaking figure of merit, the Monte Carlo method with its
statistical consequences, and the optimisation machinery --- Pareto
dominance, Gaussian-process surrogates and the active-learning loop.
Standard derivations are cited rather than repeated~\cite{duderstadt_hamilton_1976,stacey_2018};
emphasis falls on the points where theory shapes decisions taken later.

\section{Neutron multiplication, leakage and reactivity}
\label{sec:bg-k}

The multiplication factor is the ratio of neutron populations in
successive fission generations. In an infinite, homogeneous-boundary
system no neutron escapes and the balance defines $k_\infty$; in a
finite system leakage subtracts from the balance and the observable
quantity is $k_{\mathrm{eff}} < k_\infty$. Figure~\ref{fig:bg-k}
shows this hierarchy measured on the thesis model itself: the pin cell
and the assembly, both under reflective boundaries, differ only through
intra-assembly structure ($1.296 \rightarrow 1.288$), while the step to
the 32-assembly core with its reflector and vacuum boundary opens the
radial and axial leakage paths ($\rightarrow 1.221$). Reactivity,
$\rho = (k-1)/k$, must be positive at beginning of life (BOL) by enough
margin to survive depletion, yet bounded above so the excess remains
controllable; both requirements enter the optimisation directly as the
constraint $1.02 \le k_{\mathrm{BOL}} \le 1.35$. Because the
optimisation workhorse is the \emph{assembly} under reflective
boundaries, end of cycle cannot be defined at $k_\infty = 1$: the
finite core it represents loses reactivity to leakage, and the
criterion becomes the leakage-corrected target
$k_\mathrm{target} = k_\infty / k_{\mathrm{eff}}$ introduced in
Section~\ref{sec:meth-ktarget}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{images/bg_k_hierarchy.pdf}
  \caption{The multiplication ladder of the thesis model at reference
  conditions. Each geometric step opens a leakage path; the
  core-to-assembly ratio defines the leakage-corrected end-of-cycle
  target used throughout the optimisation.}
  \label{fig:bg-k}
\end{figure}

\section{Depletion, burnup and cycle length}
\label{sec:bg-depletion}

As fissile material is consumed and absorbing fission products
accumulate, $k_\infty$ falls with burnup $B$, the thermal energy
released per unit mass of heavy metal (MWd/kgHM). The isotopic
evolution obeys the coupled Bateman equations, solved here by OpenMC's
depletion module with transport-updated reaction rates on an adaptive
burnup schedule. Because the assembly specific power
$P_\mathrm{spec}$ is constant in this model, burnup maps linearly to
time and the cycle length in effective full-power days follows as
$\mathrm{EFPD} = 10^3 B_\mathrm{EOC} / P_\mathrm{spec}$.
Figure~\ref{fig:bg-dep} sketches the resulting life curve and the three
horizons that structure the campaigns: the reactivity-defined end of
cycle where $k_\infty(B)$ crosses $k_\mathrm{target}$; the
gadolinia hold-down and burnout that reshape the early curve; and the
accident-tolerant-fuel (ATF) discharge limit that may censor the
reactivity-defined cycle altogether --- the mechanism behind both the
censoring bookkeeping of Campaign~2 and the objective saturation
observed in Campaign~3.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{images/bg_gd_depletion.pdf}
  \caption{Illustrative reactivity-versus-burnup curves. The absorber
  suppresses BOL reactivity and burns out; cycle length is set by the
  $k_\mathrm{target}$ crossing unless the ATF discharge limit
  intervenes first.}
  \label{fig:bg-dep}
\end{figure}

\section{Power peaking}
\label{sec:bg-peaking}

Thermal margins are governed not by average power but by the hottest
fuel rod. The radial (enthalpy-rise) peaking factor used here is
\begin{equation}
  F_{\Delta H} \;=\; \frac{\max_i q_i}{\bar q},
  \label{eq:fdh}
\end{equation}
the maximum pin power relative to the assembly mean
(Fig.~\ref{fig:bg-pin}). Guide tubes displace fuel and locally boost
their neighbours through added moderation; gadolinia pins depress their
own power and load the pins around them. Two properties of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:fdh} matter later: it is evaluated at BOL on the fresh
assembly, where zoning and absorber effects are strongest; and it is a
\emph{maximum over many estimated quantities}, which under Monte Carlo
evaluation makes it a biased order statistic
(Section~\ref{sec:bg-mc}).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.72\linewidth]{images/bg_pin_power.pdf}
  \caption{Synthetic pin-power map on the thesis lattice, defining
  $F_{\Delta H}$. Grey positions are guide tubes; ringed pins carry
  gadolinia and depress their own power --- the reason a maximum-based
  estimator is structurally blind to the absorber
  (Section~\ref{sec:res-importance}).}
  \label{fig:bg-pin}
\end{figure}

\section{Gadolinia burnable absorbers}
\label{sec:bg-gd}

Excess BOL reactivity must be held down without spending control-rod
worth. Gadolinia (Gd$_2$O$_3$) mixed into selected fuel pins does this
through the extreme thermal absorption of $^{155}$Gd and $^{157}$Gd
(Fig.~\ref{fig:bg-xs}): poisoned pellets are optically black, so
absorption proceeds from the pellet surface inward and the hold-down
\emph{duration} is set by geometry as much as by content --- the
self-shielding that industrial practice exploits by concentrating the
poison in a limited number of rods~\cite{gd_enriched_2021}. Three
consequences recur in the results: reactivity authority scales with the
total absorber inventory (concentration $\times$ pin count), so a fixed
pin pattern bounds it; the residual end-of-life penalty of natural
gadolinia is small~\cite{ba_snf_2001}; and the local power depression
couples the absorber to the peaking objective in a way the
maximum-based estimator cannot see.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{images/bg_thermal_xs.pdf}
  \caption{Thermal (2200\,m/s) absorption cross sections. The two odd
  gadolinium isotopes absorb two to five orders of magnitude more
  strongly than the fuel nuclides, the basis of the black-absorber and
  self-shielding behaviour.}
  \label{fig:bg-xs}
\end{figure}

\section{The Monte Carlo method and its statistics}
\label{sec:bg-mc}

OpenMC solves the transport eigenvalue problem by power iteration over
fission generations: a batch of neutron histories is tracked, fission
sites seed the next batch, and tallies accumulate over \emph{active}
batches once the source has converged, the first \emph{inactive}
batches being discarded. Source convergence is monitored through the
Shannon entropy of the fission-site distribution, stationary once the
spatial source has settled --- the diagnostic added to every
Campaign-3 evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:res-entropy}).

Every tallied quantity is a statistical estimate. Two properties drive
the methodology (Fig.~\ref{fig:bg-mc}). First, the standard deviation
of a tally contracts as $1/\sqrt{N}$ with the number of active
histories; panel~(a) shows the law anchored to the thesis's own
measured fidelity ladder for $F_{\Delta H}$. Second --- and less
familiar --- an objective defined as the \emph{maximum} over many
noisy cells is an extreme order statistic and is biased
\emph{upward}: the winning cell is preferentially one that fluctuated
high. Panel~(b) makes the mechanism visible on a nearly flat field of
264 cells: at the per-cell noise of the Campaign-2 fidelity the
estimated maximum sits far above the true one, and, critically,
averaging over seeds narrows the distribution but does not move it ---
bias is removed only by more histories per evaluation. The bias also
grows as the true field flattens (more near-ties, more chances for an
upward fluctuation), i.e.\ it penalises most exactly the designs a
peaking-minimising optimiser should prefer. This mechanism, quantified
on the real campaign in Section~\ref{sec:res-noise}, is the origin of
the ranking inversion that motivates the two-stage selection
methodology.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{images/bg_mc_noise.pdf}
  \caption{Monte Carlo statistics of the peaking estimator.
  (a)~$1/\sqrt{N}$ contraction, anchored to the measured ladder of this
  work. (b)~Simulated distribution of the maximum over 264 noisy cells
  on a nearly flat field: at high per-cell noise the estimator is
  strongly biased upward, and seed-averaging cannot remove the bias.}
  \label{fig:bg-mc}
\end{figure}

\section{Reduced-order proxies and rank fidelity}
\label{sec:bg-proxy}

An optimiser driven by a cheap proxy inherits the proxy's
\emph{ordering}, not its absolute accuracy. The operative quantity is
therefore rank correlation --- Spearman's
$\rho = 1 - 6\sum d_i^2/[n(n^2-1)]$ over paired rankings --- and its
weakness is systematic: proxy--truth correlation degrades near the
optimum, where designs crowd together and small structural errors
reorder them. Two responses exist: fuse the fidelities statistically
through a learned discrepancy~\cite{kennedy_ohagan_2000,forrester_2007},
or measure the true quantity directly where its cost permits. Both are
exercised in this thesis (Sections~\ref{sec:meth-core-objective}
and~\ref{sec:res-corevalidation}).

\section{Multi-objective optimisation}
\label{sec:bg-moo}

With two competing objectives no single optimum exists. Design $a$
\emph{dominates} $b$ if it is at least as good in both objectives and
strictly better in one; the non-dominated subset of a design archive is
its Pareto set, and the corresponding attainment staircase in objective
space is the Pareto front (Fig.~\ref{fig:bg-pareto}). Progress of a
front is summarised by the \emph{hypervolume}: the objective-space
measure dominated by the front relative to a fixed reference point ---
the scalar whose stagnation forms half of the empirical stopping rule
of Section~\ref{sec:meth-loop}. The search engine is
NSGA-II~\cite{deb_nsga2_2002}, which evolves a population under
non-dominated sorting with crowding-distance selection to spread
solutions along the front.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth]{images/bg_pareto_hv.pdf}
  \caption{Dominance, the Pareto front and hypervolume in the objective
  orientation of this thesis (cycle length maximised, $F_{\Delta H}$
  minimised; the peaking axis is inverted so that better is upward).}
  \label{fig:bg-pareto}
\end{figure}

\section{Gaussian-process surrogates}
\label{sec:bg-gp}

A Gaussian process (GP) places a prior over functions, fully specified
by a mean and a covariance kernel; conditioning on evaluated designs
yields a posterior whose mean interpolates the data and whose variance
quantifies ignorance away from it~\cite{rasmussen_gp_2006}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:bg-gp}). Two kernel features carry weight here. An
\emph{automatic relevance determination} kernel learns one length-scale
per design variable, so a variable along which the response is flat is
assigned a large length-scale --- the property exploited by the
variable-importance analysis. A \emph{white-noise} component absorbs
the evaluation noise; its i.i.d.\ assumption across designs is exactly
what a shared random seed violates, motivating the per-design seeding
policy of Campaign~3, and its fitted magnitude upper-bounds the true
Monte Carlo noise, the excess measuring residual model misfit
(Section~\ref{sec:res-importance}).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{images/bg_gp.pdf}
  \caption{Gaussian-process regression on noisy evaluations: posterior
  mean, 95\% predictive band, and the growth of uncertainty away from
  data that active learning exploits.}
  \label{fig:bg-gp}
\end{figure}

\section{Design of experiments and active learning}
\label{sec:bg-al}

The surrogate is only as good as its training set. The initial design
of experiments uses Latin hypercube sampling~\cite{mckay_lhs_1979},
which stratifies every variable individually and fills a
high-dimensional box far more evenly than uniform random sampling at
equal budget. From there the campaign follows the dual-stage
active-learning loop of Fig.~\ref{fig:bg-al}: the expensive code
evaluates a batch, the GP is retrained on the \emph{whole} cumulative
archive, NSGA-II searches the surrogate, and a small infill batch of
its proposals returns to the expensive code --- with the stopping rule
applied between blocks and finalists confirmed at high fidelity, the
two-tier principle that recurs throughout the thesis.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{images/bg_al_loop.pdf}
  \caption{The dual-stage surrogate-assisted active-learning loop as
  implemented, including the between-block stopping rule and the
  high-fidelity confirmation stage.}
  \label{fig:bg-al}
\end{figure}
